name: Apache Kafka
summary: The open-source distributed log that most event streaming is built on, or built to be compatible with.
intro: Kafka stores each topic as a set of partitions, and each partition as a series of segment files on a broker’s disk. A producer picks the partition by hashing the record’s key, so every event for one customer lands, in order, in the same partition. Each partition is copied to several brokers: one leader takes the writes and the followers replicate them. Records stay until the retention limit (seven days by default) or, with log compaction, until a newer record with the same key replaces them.

Since Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) a cluster runs entirely in KRaft mode: a few controller nodes keep the cluster’s metadata in their own Raft-replicated log, and the separate ZooKeeper ensemble that older versions needed is gone. Around the core sit Kafka Connect, a framework of ready-made source and sink connectors for databases, object stores and warehouses, and Kafka Streams, a Java library for stateful stream processing. Share groups (“Queues for Kafka”), production-ready since 4.2, let many consumers split the records of the same partitions and acknowledge them one by one, like a queue.
strengths: Sequential disk writes and batching give very high throughput on ordinary hardware
Consumers can rewind to any retained offset, so a new service or a fixed bug can reprocess history
The biggest ecosystem in streaming: Connect, Streams, Flink, Spark, and a protocol that Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud, Redpanda and Azure Event Hubs all speak
Log compaction turns a topic into a durable “latest value per key” changelog
limits: Running it yourself is real work: partition counts, replication, rebalancing, disk sizing and upgrades; many teams pay for a managed service instead
The partition count caps parallelism (one consumer per partition in a group), and adding partitions remaps keys and breaks per-key ordering
No per-message routing, delays or priorities; that logic lives in your consumers
Long retention on broker disks is expensive unless you set up tiered storage (production-ready since 3.9) with a remote-storage plugin

story: Around 2010, LinkedIn had two kinds of data that didn’t fit together. Databases held users and connections, but a much bigger stream of events (page views, searches, clicks, server metrics) had to reach Hadoop for offline analysis and live systems like search and newsfeed at the same time. The messaging systems of the day, such as ActiveMQ, focused on rich delivery guarantees, were hard to scale and slowed down badly when unread messages piled up. Log collectors like Facebook’s Scribe moved data in bulk to Hadoop but couldn’t feed anything in real time.

Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao built Kafka to do both: take in billions of events a day and let any number of systems read them, in real time or hours later. They described it in a 2011 paper at the NetDB workshop. Kreps named it after Franz Kafka because it was “a system optimized for writing” and he liked the author’s work. LinkedIn open-sourced it in January 2011, and in 2014 the three creators left to found Confluent around it.

Kafka changed how companies think about data movement. Instead of point-to-point pipelines between every pair of systems, many now publish events once to a central log, and every other system subscribes.

choices.choice: An append-only log on disk instead of a message queue
choices.why: Writing to the end of a file and reading it in order is the fastest thing a disk does. Keeping data for days, rather than deleting it on delivery, lets slow consumers, batch jobs and new systems replay history.
The broker doesn’t record which messages each consumer has seen, so serving one more consumer costs almost nothing, and a consumer can rewind just by changing its offset.

choices.choice: Partitions as the unit of scale and order
choices.why: Splitting a topic into partitions spreads it over many machines. Ordering is promised only within a partition, which is enough for “all events for one user, in order” without a global bottleneck.
Kafka relies on the OS page cache instead of its own cache, and on `sendfile` to copy data from disk to network without passing through the application, which is a large part of why it’s fast.

timeline.text: Built at LinkedIn to move activity data and metrics
Open-sourced in January; NetDB paper; enters the Apache Incubator in July
Graduates to a top-level Apache project in October
Exactly-once delivery and transactions arrive in 0.11; version 1.0 follows in November
KIP-500 proposes replacing ZooKeeper with Kafka’s own Raft-based quorum (KRaft)
Kafka 4.0 runs without ZooKeeper entirely and previews queues (KIP-932)
